<!-- slide · theme step 1 -->
## Build Your Own Theme · Step 1 — The Palette {.smaller}

[Theme builder · tokens]{.eyebrow}

### Name your colours once

Pick a few story colours and some quiet neutrals, and bind them to named constants. These are your design tokens. Nothing is styled yet, you're just deciding the vocabulary every later figure will speak.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "2-5"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.4
# five story colours + neutrals — your design tokens
GREEN, BLUE, AMBER = "#379A8B", "#006BA2", "#EBB434"
RED, PURPLE        = "#B4405F", "#9A607F"
INK, MUTED, GREY   = "#211f1a", "#666666", "#B3B3B3"
LINE, CREAM        = "#D9D9D9", "#FAF9F7"

swatch = [("GREEN", GREEN), ("BLUE", BLUE), ("AMBER", AMBER), ("RED", RED), ("PURPLE", PURPLE)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.4))
for i, (name, hexv) in enumerate(swatch):
    y = len(swatch) - 1 - i
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((0, y), 1.1, 0.8, color=hexv))
    ax.text(1.3, y + 0.4, name, va="center", fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    ax.text(2.8, y + 0.4, hexv, va="center", color=MUTED)
ax.set_xlim(0, 4.5); ax.set_ylim(0, len(swatch)); ax.axis("off")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · theme step 2 -->
## Build Your Own Theme · Step 2 — Named Ramps {.smaller}

[Theme builder · ramps]{.eyebrow}

### Dark-to-light gradients for many categories

Five colours run out fast with many-category or continuous data. Add named **ramps**, each a dark-to-light gradient you can pick by name. The full theme ships nine; three are shown here.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "2-6"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 4.0
# nine named dark→light ramps (three shown) for category & sequential data
ECON = {
    "chicago":  ["#141F52", "#3C4A8C", "#7480C4", "#B7BEEB", "#EBEDFA"],
    "hongkong": ["#169C7F", "#4FC2A8", "#8FD9C9", "#C7ECE4", "#E9FCF8"],
    "newyork":  ["#F9C31F", "#FAD25A", "#FBE08C", "#FDEFC2", "#FEF8E6"],
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.0))
for j, (name, ramp) in enumerate(ECON.items()):       # one row per ramp
    for i, hexv in enumerate(ramp):
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((i, -j), 0.95, 0.9, color=hexv, ec=CREAM, lw=0.6))
    ax.text(-0.3, -j + 0.45, name, ha="right", va="center", family="IBM Plex Mono", color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 5); ax.set_ylim(-len(ECON) + 0.5, 1); ax.axis("off")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · theme step 3 -->
## Build Your Own Theme · Step 3 — Continuous Colormaps {.smaller}

[Theme builder · cmaps]{.eyebrow}

### Turn the ramps into matplotlib colormaps

Heatmaps and stacked areas need a *continuous* gradient. `LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list` interpolates any list of hexes into a colormap: one sequential, one diverging, one full-spectrum.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "4-7"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 3.4
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap

# interpolate the ramps into continuous colormaps
econ_cmap      = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("econ_chicago", ECON["chicago"])
econ_diverging = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("econ_div", [BLUE, CREAM, RED])
econ_spectrum  = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
    "econ_spectrum", [ECON["chicago"][1], ECON["hongkong"][1], ECON["newyork"][1], RED])

grad = np.linspace(0, 1, 256).reshape(1, -1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.0, 3.4))
demos = [(econ_cmap, "econ_cmap · sequential"),
         (econ_diverging, "econ_diverging · blue ↔ red"),
         (econ_spectrum, "econ_spectrum · blue → red")]
for a, (cm, label) in zip(axes, demos):
    a.imshow(grad, aspect="auto", cmap=cm); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
    a.set_title(label, loc="left", family="IBM Plex Mono", fontsize=10, color=INK, pad=4)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · theme step 4 -->
## Build Your Own Theme · Step 4 — Register the Font {.smaller}

[Theme builder · font]{.eyebrow}

### Tell matplotlib about the .ttf files

The repo ships the IBM Plex Mono `.ttf` files. Walk the folder, hand each file to matplotlib's font manager, and remember the family name. A fallback keeps the render alive if the folder ever moves.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "5-11"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 4.0
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.font_manager as fm

# register the bundled .ttf files so matplotlib knows the family by name
font_dir = Path("fonts/IBM_Plex_Mono")
if font_dir.exists():
    for ttf in font_dir.glob("*.ttf"):
        fm.fontManager.addfont(str(ttf))
    MONO = "IBM Plex Mono"
else:
    MONO = "DejaVu Sans Mono"          # safe fallback

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.0)); ax.axis("off")
ax.text(0.5, 0.70, "IBM Plex Mono", ha="center", fontsize=30, fontweight="bold", color=GREEN, family=MONO)
ax.text(0.5, 0.45, 'ax.set_title("BRCA1 expression")', ha="center", fontsize=12, color=MUTED, family=MONO)
ax.text(0.5, 0.25, "now available everywhere by name", ha="center", fontsize=11, color=GREY, family=MONO, style="italic")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · theme step 5 -->
## Build Your Own Theme · Step 5 — Set Defaults Once {.smaller}

[Theme builder · rcParams]{.eyebrow}

### One rcParams call, inherited forever

A single `rcParams.update` makes the cream canvas, muted axes, dropped spines, and IBM Plex Mono the matplotlib default. Every figure after this line starts styled, with no per-chunk boilerplate.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "4-10"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 4.2
import matplotlib as mpl

# set every default once — later figures inherit it, no per-plot styling
mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": CREAM, "axes.facecolor": CREAM, "savefig.facecolor": CREAM,
    "font.family":      MONO,
    "axes.edgecolor":   LINE,  "axes.labelcolor":   MUTED,
    "xtick.color":      MUTED, "ytick.color":       MUTED,
    "axes.spines.top":  False, "axes.spines.right": False,
})

genes = ["BRCA1", "TP53", "EGFR", "MYC", "KRAS"]; vals = [72, 58, 85, 63, 91]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.2))
ax.barh(genes[::-1], vals[::-1], color=GREEN, height=0.62)
for i, v in enumerate(vals[::-1]):
    ax.text(v + 1, i, str(v), va="center", fontsize=10, color=MUTED)
ax.set_xlim(0, 105); ax.xaxis.set_visible(False)
for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("EVERY DEFAULT SET, NOTHING REPEATED", fontweight="bold", color=INK, loc="left", pad=10)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · theme payoff -->
## The Whole Theme in One Line {.smaller}

[Theme builder · the payoff]{.eyebrow}

### `from genomics_course.theme import *`

You've just seen the inside of `theme.py`: palette, ramps, colormaps, font, rcParams. The deck never re-declares any of it. It imports the same module, and every figure inherits the look.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 4.2
from genomics_course.theme import *   # palette + ramps + cmaps + font + rcParams

# every figure now starts publication-ready — no styling needed
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 60)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.2))
for k, c in zip((1, 1.6, 2.2), (GREEN, BLUE, AMBER)):
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x * 0.6) * k + k, lw=2.4, color=c)
ax.set_title("ONE IMPORT, PUBLICATION-READY", fontweight="bold", color=INK, loc="left")
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax.set_ylabel("amplitude")
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
The recipe is **palette → ramps → colormaps → font → rcParams → one import line**. Define it once; every figure in Day 1 through Day 3, and in your own work, shares the same identity.
:::
